Q: Meaning of `command < <(command)`? A:

The command yq '.coolActions[]' sample.yaml outputs "a stream" of text.

The <(...) bit can be called the "process substitution", and it takes the stream and places it in a temporary file and returns the path of that temporary file.

So one can think that <(some_command1) evaluates to temp_file1.txt .

readarray is expected to be used with the redirection operator (the < operator), since it's designed to consume standard input, like input from keyboard, but we've got a file that we get from the process substitution. The redirect operator expects a file after it, like so: < file1.txt. So one can think about some valid use of readarray as follows: readarray array_name1 < temp_or_non_temp_file.txt

The < when taken into consideration separately is called a redirect operator, and can be used with things like taking a file and passing it as the input to the command instead of the input of the keyboard. Like, some command might wait for keyboard input, but command < file1.txt treats file1.txt as the input to the command instead of keyboard input.

Please let me know if you have any questions. : )

Q: Yum crashed with a keyboard interrupt error A:

Your yum looks for python2. Let's use 'alternatives' to switch between pythons2 and python3.

  • run --> sudo alternatives --config python
  • Enter to keep the current selection[+], or type selection number:

If you don't configure it. How to do that?

  • sudo alternatives --install /usr/bin/python python /usr/local/bin/python3.8 60

  • sudo alternatives --install /usr/bin/python python /usr/bin/python2 50

Q: Can I have scalac warnings fail compilation when run from the SBT command line but not from the IDE (IntelliJ IDEA)? A:

IDEA sets the idea.managed system property to true when it runs SBT. The build can use this property to only add "-Werror" to scalacOptions when it is unset or not true.

scalacOptions ++= Seq("-Wunused")
scalacOptions ++= (if (sys.props("idea.managed") == "true") Nil else Seq("-Werror"))

With this configuration, the compilation will fail when the build is run from the terminal, on CI, or any other environment outside of the IDEA IDE. However, compilation will succeed when run in IDEA.

Q: Devel::Cover interpreting hash access as false A:

I do believe you found a bug. Without going too far into the technical route, it is worth noting that Devel::Cover works by inspecting Perl's compiled operation tree, usually called the optree.

For a defined-or expression like $a // $b, the compiled optree will be something along these lines:

1  <|> dor(other->9) K/1 ->4
2     <0> padsv[$a] s ->1
3     <0> padsv[$b] s ->4
4  ...

In less internal terms, this means roughly:

evaluate $a
run the defined-or op
    if $a is defined: skip the RHS
    otherwise: evaluate $b
continue after the expression

So $a is already visible on the stack, but $b still needs to be evaluated. In order to collect data about the RHS when short circuiting is not possible (LHS is not defined), Devel::Cover needs to wait for this evaluation. It does that by temporarily hijacking the next operation pointer (represented by -> above) held by the RHS evaluation op, creating a small breakpoint there, just to capture the value and then continue.

Here is where, in my interpretation, the bug resides. For simple scalars, the next op is clearly declared. But $b{x} may be transformed into a wrapper for hash access. In B::Concise output, that can look something like this:

1  <|> dor(other->n) K/1 ->4
2     <0> padsv[$a] s ->1
-     <1> ex-helem sK/2 ->-
3        <+> multideref($b{"x"}) sK ->4
4  ...

The ex-helem op is the wrapper for hash element access. The real operation that evaluates $b{x} is the child op (instruction 3 in this example). So when this happens, the useful next op belongs to the real operation inside the wrapper (3, pointing to 4 in this example).

The wrapper's own next pointer (-) is part of the static optree, but not really part of the runtime path. It can point to structural parts of the tree, such as the surrounding statement sequence, instead of pointing to the operation that runs after $b{x} has actually produced its value.

I've created a PR to make Devel::Cover visit the wrapper and extract the proper next operation. I'll keep this answer updated if that is actually the case.
